d.title: A retriever that finds nothing returns an empty list and a 200
d.caption: This is the whole reason LLM observability is a separate subject. **A database that cannot find a row raises an exception; a retriever that cannot find a chunk returns an empty list and the request succeeds.** So error rate, latency, saturation and traffic are all necessary and **none of them fire**. The practical consequence: correctness has to be instrumented deliberately, as its own signal with its own storage and its own alerts, because nothing you already run will tell you.

nodes.label: So instrument correctness deliberately
nodes.sub: its own signal, storage and alerts

d.title: Three properties, each breaking a different debugging habit
d.caption: **Non-determinism** means you cannot reproduce a failure by replaying the input — 1.2 measured logits differing by batch composition alone. **Compound systems** mean a RAG answer passes through six stages and the output cannot say which one broke. **Silent drift** means nothing crashes when your corpus triples or the provider swaps the weights behind an alias. Together they remove replay, bisection and crash reports: the three things debugging normally relies on.

cells.text: replay - the same input does not reproduce the failure
bisection - six stages, and the output names none of them
crash reports - a tripled corpus raises nothing at all

d.title: Four signals, and what each one can answer
d.caption: The cardinality column is what decides retention policy. **Metrics are low-cardinality numbers over time and cheap to keep forever**, which is why trends live there. Logs and traces are high-cardinality and have to be sampled or expired. Evals sit in the middle and are the LLM-specific addition — and the questions column shows why they cannot be folded into any of the other three.
cells: is something wrong, and since when?

cells.text: where in the pipeline did it break?

d.title: A metric comes from the machinery; an eval score comes from the meaning
d.caption: A metric is derived from counts, durations and bytes. **An eval score is derived from the meaning of a request and its response**, which is why it does not fit in the metrics pillar even though it ends up on a dashboard as a number: faithfulness at 0.91 is the output of a judge with a rubric and a version, not a counter. The operational consequence is specific — **an eval score must be joinable to the trace that produced it.** A faithfulness score with no trace is a number you cannot act on.

nodes.label: Produced by a judge with a rubric
So it must join to its trace
A score with no trace is unactionable

d.title: Five quality metrics, and where each number comes from
d.caption: The third column is the one that decides whether a metric is affordable. **Answer accuracy needs an offline regression set and runs nightly**; faithfulness and relevancy need an LLM judge on sampled live traces, which 10.11 prices. **Refusal rate and thumbs-down need no model at all** — a regex and a product-UI join — which makes them the two to instrument first. The alert conditions are deliberately relative rather than absolute, because 10.12 shows an absolute threshold pages on noise.

cells.text: the product UI, joined to the trace

d.title: Six retrieval metrics, and the two that come free from the span
d.caption: Most of this layer needs a judge or a labelled set. **Two do not: empty-retrieval rate and mean top-1 score come straight off the retriever span**, cost nothing, and are the earliest signals in the whole system — 10.13's incident shows empty retrieval going from 0.4% to 11.2% while faithfulness stayed at 0.95. Instrument those two before buying anything, because they catch an index or embedding change within the hour.

d.title: Ten terms, and the one that makes a trace a tree
d.caption: A **trace** is everything that happened for one request. A **span** is one unit of work inside it. **The parent link is what makes a trace a tree** — without it you have a flat list of timed events and none of §03's analysis is available. The **root span's duration is the user-visible latency**, which is the one number a user could have measured themselves. And **context propagation** is what keeps the tree intact across threads, processes and HTTP calls — the thing that breaks first in practice.

nodes.sub: one unit of work inside it

nodes.label: Root span
nodes.sub: its duration is the user's latency

d.title: Span kind looks like metadata and is load-bearing
d.caption: **`SERVER` on the root marks where the user's clock starts; `CLIENT` marks every call out of your process.** That split answers the first question of any latency investigation — *how much of this is ours?* In 10.5's worked trace the `CLIENT` spans total 2,900 of 3,834 ms. It also drives aggregations: 10.7 rolls token counts up by filtering on `kind == CLIENT`, which is correct and **fragile in a way worth seeing**, because one mis-kinded span silently changes a cost figure.

nodes.label: How much of this is ours?
So one mis-kinded span moves a cost figure

d.title: Three analyses that only exist because the trace is a tree
d.caption: A flat list of timed events supports none of these. **Self time** is a span's own work with its children subtracted — in 10.5's trace `retrieve` is 624 ms with 617 ms of children, so its self time is 7 ms and the wrapper is doing nothing but coordinating. **The critical path** matters because with concurrency the sum of span durations exceeds the total. And **blame by stage** — "76% was the model, 20% retrieval" — falls straight out of the structure.

with concurrency the span durations sum to more than the total

d.title: The waterfall, and three things it settles
d.caption: **`llm.generate` owns 75.7% of total latency**, which means work that does not start with streaming, a shorter prompt or a smaller model is work on the wrong 24%. `retrieve` is 624 ms with 617 ms of children, so **its self time is 7 ms** — the wrapper coordinates and nothing else. And `rerank` at 259 ms is **nearly as expensive as the search it reranks** (274 ms): that is the price of a cross-encoder, and 6.1 measured that it can also make results worse.

d.title: Eight span types, and what each must carry
d.caption: The pattern across the rows: **a span must carry whatever you would need to reconstruct the decision it made.** The retrieve span needs the index *version*, not just its name, and the scores as well as the chunk IDs — because 10.13's diagnosis turns on `above_threshold` being 0 while `returned` was 20. The llm.generate span needs the **exact version pin**, which §02 argues is the single highest-value attribute in the schema.

d.title: Three attributes that earn their place above all others
d.caption: Each one turns an unanswerable question into a comparison. **`chat-large` is not a version and `chat-large-2026-03-11` is** — when a provider rolls an alias, only the pinned comparison catches it. **Prompts change more often than code** and frequently outside version control, so a template ID or hash is the only way to attribute a quality change to one. And **every re-index is a deploy**: naming the index `support-docs-v4` rather than `support-docs` makes that deploy visible in every trace.

cells.text: an alias roll is invisible without it - and it is one comparison

d.title: A tracer is three ideas, and nothing else is needed
d.caption: **The stack gives you parent links, and parent links give you the tree** — `self.stack[-1]` is the parent of whatever you open next. **Two clock reads give you duration**, which gives you both the waterfall and self time. And **`**attrs` gives you the searchable dimensions** — model, index, token counts, scores. That is the whole mechanism: everything in 10.4 and 10.5 falls out of a list, a clock and a dict.

nodes.label: The searchable dimensions
nodes.sub: which is what makes it useful

d.title: Five things production adds, and the one that corrupts data silently
d.caption: The first row is the one that matters most and looks least important. **A plain list attribute is shared across tasks, so two concurrent requests interleave their stacks and the tree becomes nonsense** — not empty, not erroring: nonsense, with spans attached to the wrong parents. `contextvars.ContextVar` is the fix and it is a one-line change that nothing in a single-request test will reveal.

d.title: The conventions buy correctness, not only portability
d.caption: The usual argument is portability — instrument once, change vendor later — and it is true and the weaker argument. **The stronger one came out of building the tracer: rolling up token counts by filtering on span kind overstated cost by 63% after an ordinary refactor**, because a span that should have been `INTERNAL` was `CLIENT`. A name that means exactly one thing is a name you can aggregate on safely, and an ad-hoc name is not.

nodes.label: Roll up tokens by span kind
A standard name means one thing

d.title: Two model fields, and only one of them changes
d.caption: You log what you **requested** and what the provider **responded with**. When a provider moves an alias, **only the second changes**: you asked for `chat-large` yesterday and today, and yesterday that was `chat-large-2026-03-11`. So log both and alert when the response model is not the version you pinned — **one comparison on one attribute.** It also reframes the investigation: a quality metric tells you something got worse and leaves you hunting; this tells you the cause directly.

nodes.label: It names the cause, not the symptom

d.title: Eight tools, and one category error to avoid
d.caption: The last two rows are not competitors to the others. **Ragas and DeepEval compute metrics: they do not store traces, have no UI, and do not alert** — they are the thing a backend calls. Treating them as a platform choice leads to the wrong question (*Ragas or Langfuse?*) instead of the right one (*which backend, and which metric library inside it?*). And 9.17 applies here too: the metric **implementation** determines the number.
cells: one pane with your other services

d.title: Five defaults, and the asymmetry they all exploit
d.caption: Every row is the same trade: **metadata is small and payloads are not.** So keep 100% of metadata and 5–10% of prompt and chunk text; keep aggregated metrics forever and payloads for 14–30 days, because incidents are found in weeks and trends in months. The truncation rule is the neatest statement of the principle: **you rarely need chunk 5 in full, and you always need to know which chunk it was.**

d.title: Head sampling keeps a random 5% and throws away the failures
d.caption: **Head sampling decides at the start** — keep 5% — which is cheap and trivially implemented, and because the decision precedes the outcome it keeps a random 5% **including a random 5% of your failures**. Tail sampling decides after the request finishes, once you know it was slow, errored or scored badly. With errors, slow requests and low scores at 6.7% of traffic combined, tail sampling keeps **all of them** for about the same storage as head sampling at 5% keeps nothing in particular.

d.title: Three tiers, and the rule that comes first
d.caption: **Never block the response on a judge.** It adds a second of latency and a second failure mode for a score you can compute afterwards from the stored trace. Below that: **deterministic checks are free, so run them on everything** — empty retrieval, missing citation, malformed JSON and refusal patterns need no model. And sample for the judge, **stratified**: random 2% plus 100% of thumbs-down plus 100% of low-similarity retrievals, so the budget lands where the failures are.

d.title: A judge call costs 107% of the generation it scores
d.caption: A faithfulness judge has to see **the context** to decide whether a claim is supported and **the answer** to find the claims — so its input is the generation's input plus the generation's output. That puts a judge call at **107% of the generation it scores**, which means judging every request **more than doubles your model spend**. Which is both why 'score a sample' is the only affordable policy and why the cheap tier matters: a citation check and a refusal regex cost nothing and catch a real share of failures.

nodes.label: So its input is input plus output
nodes.sub: of the call it is scoring

nodes.label: So prefer the free tier where it answers

d.title: The threshold is one line of arithmetic per alert
d.caption: **At N = 200 the 2σ band is ±3.08 points**, so a 2-point move is well inside the noise and will happen regularly with nothing wrong — an alert on it pages somebody every week for no reason, and then people stop reading alerts. The fix: take the baseline rate, take the daily sample size, compute two sigma, set the threshold there. Then add the second condition — **two days running** — because a single day at 2σ happens about one day in twenty by chance and two consecutive days is far rarer.

nodes.label: Alert on it and people stop reading

d.title: Seven alerts, and the two that need no judge
d.caption: **Empty retrieval is the earliest RAG signal there is and it needs no judge** — a counter on the retriever span. Top-1 score collapse catches an index or embedding change **within an hour**, which no quality metric does. And the response-model mismatch catches a provider alias roll immediately, which is 10.8's one-comparison alert. Three of these seven cost nothing to run and catch the failures that take longest to find by any other route.
